issues.description: The methods section reports a final sample of N = 372, but Tables 1 and 2 report N = 321 for the main analyses. This 51-person discrepancy is never explained or acknowledged anywhere in the manuscript. Additionally, 468 - 16 (missing time points) - 78 (data quality) = 374, not 372. The arithmetic for the reported final sample does not add up.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.description: The reported retention numbers imply 18 total dropouts across waves (468→458=10 lost at T2; 458→454=4 lost at T3; 454→450=4 lost at T4), but the text claims only n=16 were excluded for missing time points. Since participants who missed one wave were not invited to subsequent waves, cumulative dropout should be 18, not 16.
issues.quote: n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points

issues.description: Correlations between key study variables are extraordinarily high (e.g., T4 Compassion Fatigue–T4 Enacted Incivility r=.94; T1 Compassion Fatigue–T1 Enacted Incivility r=.85; T2 Customer Incivility–T4 Compassion Fatigue r=.85). Correlations of .94 suggest the constructs are virtually indistinguishable, severely undermining the claim that these are distinct mediator and outcome variables. The CFA comparison also shows minimal differentiation: the one-factor model (CFI=.98, TLI=.98) fits nearly as well as the four-factor model (CFI=.99, TLI=.99).
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue... T4 Enacted Incivility... .94

issues.description: The CFA model comparison statistics are incoherent. The reported degrees of freedom for alternative models (3, 2, 1) are implausible for standalone model fits with 25+ items. These may be intended as Δdf values for nested comparisons, but they are presented with RMSEA/CFI/TLI as if they are standalone models. Furthermore, the chi-square for the three-factor model (82.52) is dramatically smaller than the four-factor model (862.05), which is impossible since more constrained models must have equal or larger chi-square values.
issues.quote: a three-factor model wherein both incivility measures were set to load onto the same factor (3) = 82.52, RMSEA = .09, CFI = .98, TLI = .98), a two-factor model... (2) = 82.65, RMSEA = .10, CFI = .98, TLI = .98), and a one-factor model (1) = 8.02, RMSEA = .10, CFI = .98, TLI = .98)

issues.description: In the results text, the serial indirect effect for H4 is reported as B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01. A z-ratio of .06/.04 = 1.5 would yield p ≈ .13, not p < .01. However, Table 2 reports the same indirect effect as B = .06, SE = .02, t = 2.58, which is consistent with p < .01. The SE value in the text (.04) contradicts the SE in the table (.02).
issues.quote: Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]).

issues.subcategory: temporal separation failure in serial mediation
issues.description: The serial mediation model (H4) requires temporal ordering of incivility (T2) → negative emotions (T3) → compassion fatigue (T4) → enacted incivility (T4). However, the final mediator (compassion fatigue) and outcome (enacted incivility) are both measured at T4, eliminating the temporal separation needed for causal inference between these two variables. This undermines the longitudinal design advantage claimed throughout the paper.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 4: The positive relationship between experienced patient incivility and enacted incivility towards patients is indirect through negative emotions towards patients and compassion fatigue.

issues.description: With between-wave correlations among substantive variables in the .70-.94 range, severe multicollinearity is virtually certain. This is reflected in unstable regression coefficients (e.g., experienced incivility predicting enacted incivility flips from positive in bivariate correlations to B = -.07/-.03 in regression). The R² = .81 for enacted incivility also suggests redundancy rather than meaningful prediction.

The relative importance analysis reports that experienced incivility accounts for 24.1% of variance in enacted incivility, yet the regression coefficient is non-significant (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40). While relative importance metrics can differ from regression weights, reporting a non-significant predictor as accounting for a quarter of explained variance without acknowledging the suppression or multicollinearity driving this discrepancy is misleading.
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.subcategory: text refers to coworker incivility instead of patient incivility
issues.description: The compassion fatigue section states the study examines 'coworker incivility,' which contradicts the entire study focus on patient incivility. This appears to be a writing error but creates confusion about the theoretical framing.
issues.quote: Within the current study, we look specifically at the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue.

issues.description: Arnold & Walsh is cited as '2005' in the introduction but as '2015' in both the references and the discussion section.
issues.quote: e.g., Arnold & Walsh, 2005; Grandey et al., 2007

issues.description: Grandey et al. (2007) is misspelled as 'Grandy et al., 2007' in the first paragraph.
issues.quote: e.g., Grandy et al., 2007; Porath & Pearson, 2013

issues.subcategory: R Core Team citation year mismatch
issues.description: The text cites 'R Core Team, 2021' but the reference list entry is dated 2020.
issues.quote: we used the relaimpo package in R (Grömping, 2006)... (R Core Team, 2021)

issues.description: The patient acuity moderator variable has substantial missing data, reducing the analysis sample from N=321 to N=244 (approximately 24% data loss). The manuscript relies on listwise deletion rather than modern missing data techniques (e.g., multiple imputation, FIML). Although the authors compare demographics between groups with and without missing data, this does not rule out data being missing at random conditional on unobserved variables.
issues.quote: N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: For the patient acuity variable, 45% of missing values were due to 'incorrect responses' (values outside expected range). This is not truly 'missing' data but rather measurement failure, which raises different concerns about whether the item was understood by nearly a quarter of the sample. Combined with the blank responses (55% of missingness), this suggests the single-item measure may have been problematic for many participants.
issues.quote: responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response)

issues.description: Patient acuity is measured with a single self-report item asking nurses to estimate the percentage of 'severe' patients, referencing various acuity scales (ESI, CRIB, SOIS). These scales measure fundamentally different things in different care contexts (e.g., CRIB is for neonatal care, ESI for emergency departments). Asking nurses to mentally aggregate across diverse acuity metrics likely introduces substantial measurement error and non-comparability across respondents from different units.
issues.quote: Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools

issues.description: The Negative Emotions Scale includes only four items: aversion, disgust, anger, and fear. For measuring emotional responses to incivility, 'fear' and 'disgust' toward patients seem less face-valid than frustration, irritation, or annoyance—the emotions most commonly associated with incivility experiences. The scale may not adequately capture the relevant negative affective construct in this context.
issues.quote: The scale items consisted of four negative emotions: (a) aversion, (b) disgust, (c) anger, (d) fear.

issues.subcategory: enacted incivility item validity in healthcare
issues.description: One enacted incivility item ('Doubted one or more patient's/patient family members' judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility') may be confounded with legitimate clinical behavior. Nurses routinely assess and question patient/family judgment as part of clinical care (e.g., medication adherence, treatment decisions). This item may inflate enacted incivility scores with normative professional behavior.
issues.quote: Doubted one or more patient's/patient family members' judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility

issues.description: Despite using observational longitudinal data, the manuscript frequently uses causal or near-causal language (e.g., 'leads to,' 'impact,' 'drives,' 'effects'). The autoregressive design reduces but does not eliminate confounding, and temporal precedence alone does not establish causation. The co-measurement of compassion fatigue and enacted incivility at T4 particularly undermines causal claims for that link.
issues.quote: experiencing incivility from patients was related to increased future incivility enactment towards patients indirectly through increased negative emotions towards patients and compassion fatigue

issues.description: The only control variable is work hours. Numerous plausible confounders are unaddressed: trait negative affectivity, neuroticism, emotional labor demands, organizational climate, staffing levels, shift type (day/night), unit type, and prior mental health status. Any of these could drive the observed associations between incivility experiences, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility.
issues.quote: T2 Work Hours... T3 Work Hours

issues.description: Recruitment via personal networks, social media, and posted flyers introduces substantial self-selection bias. Nurses who frequent online support groups or who are motivated by the study description (about incivility and wellbeing) may systematically differ from the broader nursing population. The very high correlations and mean levels of incivility could partly reflect sampling of nurses particularly affected by these issues.
issues.quote: nurse/healthcare specific forums or groups within social media networks (e.g., support group for midwest ICU nurses on Facebook)

issues.description: 78 of 468 participants (16.7%) were excluded for failed data quality checks, including 56 who could not provide consistent demographic information across waves and 21 with duplicate open-ended responses suggesting collusion or repeat participation. This extremely high rate raises concerns about the quality of the remaining data from those who passed the checks but may have provided low-quality substantive responses.
issues.quote: n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality

issues.description: Inclusion criteria required full-time work in high-stakes/critical care, but the methods state 'All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time),' contradicting the full-time requirement. The verification of the critical care criterion relied largely on self-report and a subsample check of only 20 participants' O*Net descriptions.
issues.quote: All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time), worked more than one shift a week, on average

issues.description: The same path (T4 Compassion Fatigue → T4 Enacted Incivility) is B = .57, p < .001 in Table 2 (simple mediation) but B = .40, p > .05 (t = 1.74) in Table 3 (moderated mediation). The substantial change in significance between models—from the strongest predictor to non-significant—likely reflects multicollinearity and casts doubt on the robustness of the serial mediation.
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue... .57*** ... .40

issues.subcategory: suspicious correlation pattern with work hours
issues.description: In Table 1, the correlation between T1 Patient Acuity and T1 Work Hours is -.22, but T1 Patient Acuity correlates .24 with T2 Work Hours and .23 with T3 Work Hours. The sign reversal between within-wave and cross-wave correlations for the same constructs is unusual and unexplained, potentially indicating data issues.
issues.quote: T1 Patient Acuity... T1 Work Hours... -.22... T2 Work Hours... .24

issues.description: The manuscript describes an autoregressive mediation approach where T1 variables serve as controls, but the actual autoregressive (AR1) coefficients for each variable are not reported in any table. These are essential for evaluating whether the cross-lagged effects represent genuine change beyond stability and for assessing the magnitude of within-construct stability.
issues.quote: the first wave was reserved for controlling for autoregressive effects, and the subsequent waves were included for hypothesis testing

issues.description: The CFA section reports fit indices but omits factor loadings, factor intercorrelations, and residual variances. Given the extremely high bivariate correlations between constructs, the latent factor correlations from the CFA would be essential for evaluating whether the constructs are truly distinct. The absence of these values makes it impossible to evaluate discriminant validity at the latent level.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99

issues.description: Work hours are included as control variables in some regression equations but not others, and the theoretical or empirical rationale for including this specific control—and excluding other plausible controls—is never provided.

The mediation path labels are inconsistent: H2 uses 'path a × d' (incivility→negative emotions→compassion fatigue), while H4 uses 'a × b × d' for the serial mediation. The letter 'b' appears without prior definition, and the labeling system does not follow conventional notation (a-path, b-path for simple mediation).
issues.quote: the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying each stage in the serial mediation process (a × b × d)

issues.description: No pre-registration is mentioned. Given the multiple researcher degrees of freedom (which indirect effects to test, handling of missing data, choice of controls, scale shortening decisions, data quality exclusion criteria), the absence of pre-registration makes it difficult to assess the degree to which the reported analyses were confirmatory versus exploratory.

The manuscript tests simple mediation (Table 2) and moderated mediation (Table 3) separately rather than in an integrated model. The coefficient for compassion fatigue→enacted incivility changes from significant (Table 2) to non-significant (Table 3), but this instability is not discussed. The choice of which model to emphasize for conclusions reflects undisclosed analytic flexibility.

The sample is 96.64% female, which the authors acknowledge is high even for nursing (88% nationally). This extreme gender skew limits the ability to generalize findings to male nurses or to other service professions with more balanced gender compositions, yet the discussion extrapolates broadly to 'service employees.'
issues.quote: The majority of respondents were female (96.64%), with a mean age of 34.44 (SD = 5.49) years.

issues.description: The title, abstract, and discussion generalize findings to 'customers' and 'service industries,' but the sample consists exclusively of critical-care nurses in high-stakes healthcare settings. Patient-nurse relationships involve care obligations, power dynamics, and emotional contexts fundamentally different from typical customer-employee interactions (e.g., retail, hospitality).
issues.quote: These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.description: Compassion fatigue includes a secondary trauma component (vicarious experience of patient trauma), which is conceptually distinct from exhaustion caused by incivility. The manuscript treats compassion fatigue as a caregiving-specific form of burnout driven by incivility, but patient rudeness is not the same as exposure to patient suffering/trauma that drives compassion fatigue. The theoretical link between incivility as a stressor and the secondary trauma component specifically is not well articulated.
issues.quote: Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components, with employees experiencing compassion fatigue if they are experiencing either caregiving-related burnout or secondary trauma

issues.description: Administering identical surveys weekly for four weeks risks sensitization and demand characteristics. Participants may become increasingly aware of the study's focus on incivility and emotions, potentially inflating self-reported incivility enactment over time (means trend upward from T1 to T4 for most variables). This is not addressed in limitations.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.description: The R² values for compassion fatigue (.62 in Table 2, .45 in Table 3) and enacted incivility (.81 in Table 2, .71 in Table 3) are extraordinarily high for survey-based behavioral research. Combined with correlations in the .80-.94 range, these suggest either construct redundancy or inflated associations possibly due to common method variance, despite the temporal separation.

issues.description: The manuscript does not report the percentage of the total sample with missing patient acuity data. issues.quote: our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data
